summary: Describes how to express media transport over TCP using the Session Description Protocol. It defines the SDP TCP protocol identifier, a setup attribute describing how the connection is established, and a connection attribute for re-establishing a dropped connection. It is a standards-track specification.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC lets a Session Description Protocol (SDP) description specify that media travels over Transmission Control Protocol (TCP). It also says which endpoint opens the connection and whether a later exchange keeps or replaces it.

subtitle: How SDP describes media carried over TCP and negotiates which endpoint opens the connection.

tldr.problem: SDP needed a way to describe media carried over a connection-oriented transport and to say how endpoints establish or replace that connection.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 4145 defines the TCP protocol identifier and the setup and connection attributes for negotiating connection roles and reuse.
tldr.outcome: Endpoints can describe TCP media transport in SDP. RFC 4145 is a Proposed Standard updated by RFC 4572.

facts.label: Default setup roles
facts.value: active in offer, passive in answer

today: RFC 4145 is a Proposed Standard and is updated by RFC 4572. The unit metadata does not list a later RFC that obsoletes it.

sections.title: Why SDP Needed TCP Support
sections.content:
The Session Description Protocol (SDP) is a text format that describes multimedia sessions; it does not transport the session itself. Before this specification, SDP's listed transport identifiers were for unreliable, connectionless transports. Some applications instead need TCP.

TCP requires endpoints to decide which side starts a connection and when to create a new one. RFC 4145 adds a TCP protocol identifier and the setup and connection attributes to express those decisions.
sections.plainLanguage: SDP describes how a media session should work. This RFC adds the information needed when the media uses TCP, which requires a connection between endpoints.

sections.title: The TCP Protocol Identifier
sections.content:
The SDP m= line contains a protocol field. RFC 4145 defines TCP as a value for that field. Like the existing UDP identifier, TCP identifies only the transport, not the application protocol carried over it.

An m= line using TCP must also include an fmt identifier for the application-layer protocol. The media described by that line is carried using TCP.
sections.plainLanguage: The TCP value says that Transmission Control Protocol (TCP) carries the media. The description must still name the application protocol that uses it.

sections.title: The Setup Attribute
sections.content:
The setup attribute says which endpoint initiates the TCP connection. active initiates an outgoing connection; passive accepts one; actpass allows either role; and holdconn postpones establishing the connection.

The offer/answer exchange selects the roles. An active endpoint should connect to the port on the other endpoint's m= line. Its own port is irrelevant and should be 9, the discard port. By default, an offer uses active and an answer uses passive.
sections.plainLanguage: The endpoints agree who will start the connection. One side can initiate, wait for a connection, allow either choice, or delay setup.

sections.title: Reusing and Reestablishing a Connection
sections.content:
The media-level connection attribute distinguishes a new TCP connection from reuse of an existing one. Its values are new and existing. An initial offer, or one that changes the media address or port, uses new. The answer determines the result: an offer of new requires an answer of new; an offer of existing may receive either value.

When the result is existing, the exchanged addresses, ports, and setup roles do not establish a new connection. When it is new, endpoints should open a new connection and close any old connection after the exchange completes. If a connection fails and should be restored, the endpoints should negotiate again using new.
sections.plainLanguage: A later SDP exchange can keep the current connection or request a new one. If the connection fails, the endpoints negotiate a replacement before using it again.

sections.title: Examples and Other Connection-Oriented Transports
sections.content:
The RFC's examples show T.38 fax sessions. They demonstrate an endpoint accepting a connection while the other initiates it, a choice made from actpass, and reuse of an established connection. They also show how an endpoint can request a new connection when it does not know the earlier one.

The RFC recommends that specifications for other connection-oriented transports reuse the setup and connection attributes when suitable. A different transport may need different termination rules if it does not support TCP's half-close behavior.
sections.plainLanguage: The examples show how offer and answer values determine who connects. The same attributes may also suit other connection-based transports, with transport-specific rules where needed.

sections.title: Security and Registration
sections.content:
An attacker who changes setup or connection values could prevent endpoints from connecting or cause unnecessary reconnections. The RFC strongly recommends integrity protection for SDP session descriptions. For descriptions carried in SIP, it identifies S/MIME as a natural end-to-end option; other applications may use another integrity mechanism.

The RFC registers the two attributes and the TCP protocol value with IANA. It also says that new TCP media formats should have an associated MIME registration.
sections.plainLanguage: If someone changes the connection instructions, the endpoints may not connect as intended. Integrity protection helps the receiver detect changes to the SDP description.
